content.text: This recipe makes 2 sandwiches and takes about 35 minutes.

and shredded cabbage, all packed into crustless soft white bread. The contrast of crunchy crust and pillowy bread is what makes this sandwich famous.

The pork needs to be even thickness throughout or the crust will darken before the inside is cooked. Bash the cutlet to about 1.5cm using a rolling pin or meat mallet. This also helps the panko cling evenly. Fry in oil that reaches 170 to 180 degrees C. Too cool and the crumb absorbs oil. Too hot and the outside burns before the pork cooks through.

items.prepNote: 2 steaks, each about 200g, bashed to 1.5cm thickness

content.text: Place each pork steak between two sheets of cling film. Bash evenly to 1.5cm thickness using a rolling pin. Season both sides with salt and pepper.

Set up a breading station: cornflour in one shallow dish, beaten eggs in a second, panko in a third. Coat each cutlet in cornflour first, shaking off the excess. Dip into the egg, letting any extra drip off. Press firmly into the panko, making sure the whole surface is covered.
Pour the vegetable oil into a deep frying pan to a depth of about 2cm. Heat over a medium-high heat until a piece of panko dropped in sizzles immediately and rises to the surface.
Lower the cutlets into the oil. Fry for 4 minutes on each side until deep golden brown. The pork should be cooked through with no pink remaining. Lift onto a wire rack and rest for 2 minutes.
Mix the tonkatsu sauce with the worcestershire sauce in a small bowl. Spread one side of each piece of bread with Japanese mayonnaise and the other with the tonkatsu sauce mixture.
Lay shredded cabbage on the mayonnaise side. Place a cutlet on top. Close the sandwich firmly. Cut in half cleanly with a sharp knife to reveal the layers. Serve straight away.

items.symptom: The panko crust falls off during frying
items.cause: The cutlet was not pressed firmly enough into the crumb, or the flour stage was skipped
items.fix: The cornflour layer is what makes the egg stick and the egg is what makes the panko stick. Do not skip any stage. Press the panko on firmly with the palm of your hand before frying.

items.symptom: The crust is golden but the pork inside is still pink
items.cause: Oil was too hot or the cutlet was too thick
items.fix: If the crust is done but the inside is not, transfer the cutlet to an oven tray and finish in a 180 degrees C oven for 5 minutes. Next time, bash the pork thinner or lower the oil temperature.

items.cause: The sauce was added too far in advance
items.fix: Assemble and cut the sandwich just before eating. If making ahead, keep the sauce separate and add at the last moment.

content.text: The katsu sando is sold from convenience stores, department store food halls and specialist sandwich shops across Japan. The convenience store version, often wrapped tightly in plastic and eaten standing up, has become its own icon. More elaborate versions in Tokyo's fashionable depachika food halls use wagyu beef and cost significantly more. Either way, the logic is the same: a crisp katsu cutlet, a sweet-savory sauce, and soft white bread. It travels well, which is why it appears in Japanese bento boxes and train station kiosks.
